catalog_quote: Stress in Yurok nouns appears to be sensitive to syllable weight ... Throughout, L = a light syllable (short vowel, open syllable), H = a heavy syllable (short vowel, closed syllable), and H+ = the heaviest syllable type (long vowel, open or closed). (11) Stress in [HH] disyllables ... However, when a light syllable is followed by a heavy syllable, the initial syllable is usually unstressed and reduced, with stress on the final syllable, as in (12). ... (12) Final word stress in [LH] disyllables ... ko.wís ‘stick’ ... Syllables with long vowels are always stressed in Yurok, while those with closed syllables are not. Many nouns have final unstressed CVC syllables. ... (13) Initial word stress in [H+ H] disyllables (13a) cíi.sép ‘flower’ ... (2) Deciding source is a 2003 IJAL phonology article by a fieldworker — the only dedicated treatment of Yurok stress — hedged by the author as preliminary/impressionistic, hence our 'weight-hedged' kind. (3) The one clearly better-ranked description we lacked, Garrett 2014 Basic Yurok (Survey Report 16, Glottolog's 341-pp grammar), was downloaded now (open licence, Internet Archive copy) to Its sec. 1.3 (pp.14-16) states two rules: always stress a heavy syllable (long vowel, or vowel + consonant cluster) and always stress the syllable after a closed syllable, covering 'many (though not all)' words. sources.quote: 'two stress patterns explain stress in many (though not all) Yurok words. First, in Yurok a vowel in a heavy syllable is always stressed. You should always stress long vowels, and you should always stress vowels that are followed by more than one consonant. ... Second, a vowel in the syllable after a closed syllable is always stressed. In other words, the syllables before and after a consonant cluster are both stressed.' (15) 'Two Yurok stress rules (a) Always stress a heavy syllable: hoo-gech' "star", chey-ke-nee "little". (b) Always stress the syllable after a closed syllable: chey-ke-nee "l

sources.note: Glottolog's top-ranked grammar (341 pp) with an explicit stress section (1.3) by the leading current Yurok specialist; our record rested on Blevins 2003's self-described 'preliminary' nominal-stress section alone. Now downloaded: it independently states heavy (long-vowel or cluster-closed) syllables are always stressed plus a post-closed-syllable stress rule — a second primary source for weight-sensitivity and against StressTyp2's fixed: initial syllable coding.
